summary:
Charter reports from its Workplace Summit and its AI Pulse survey (more than 5,000 US-based workers who use AI at work) on the future of middle management in the AI era. The framing starts with Block CEO Jack Dorsey's March blog post arguing AI can replace managers whose main job is information routing and questioning the need for a permanent middle management layer. Charter's panelists and data push back.

Jevan Lenox, chief people officer at Writer, argued the middle layer becomes more important as the center of gravity moves down and teams make critical decisions about how to architect work. Prudential chief people and experience officer Vicki Walia described three future manager jobs: architecting work at enterprise level, managing teams, people and agents, and leading or coaching humans, summarized as managing agents but leading people.

Charter's research found 11 of the top 14 factors associated with whether people feel they benefit from AI are set by managers, such as feeling supported to experiment or being recognized for using AI well. The strongest single factor is feeling involved in how AI fits one's job, a sense of agency. Managers are 1.8 times as likely as employees to report agency (67% versus 37%). Databricks chief people officer Amy Reichanadter said agency is a theme the company reinforces with managers.

On spans of control, Lenox critiques the player-coach and startup-ification narrative: most startup managers burn out carrying management load plus complex individual work on nights and weekends, without the equity upside. Both Writer and Databricks are moving to smaller teams. Large spans work only in stable eras.

AI Pulse interviews surfaced manager stress from doing more with less; one healthcare HR manager said people were terminated because leaders overestimated AI. Role modeling that shows the work of the work builds team confidence. Prudential, with many 25 to 30 year tenured staff, launches a function-specific program called Raise Your AI Q in November.

claims.claim: AI can replace the traditional manager whose primary job was information routing, and a permanent middle management layer may not be needed
claims.attribution: Jack Dorsey, Block CEO, in a March blog post

claims.claim: Charter's AI Pulse survey covered US-based users of AI at work
Most of the top factors associated with whether people feel they benefit from using AI are factors their managers set
The factor most strongly linked to feeling you benefit from AI use is feeling involved in how AI fits your job (agency)
Managers are far more likely than their employees to say they have agency over how AI fits their work
The middle layer of management becomes more important in a world of agentic workers and blended teams because teams architect the work
claims.attribution: Jevan Lenox, chief people officer, Writer

claims.claim: Middle managers will have three jobs: architecting work at the enterprise level, managing teams, people and agents, and leading and coaching humans
claims.attribution: Vicki Walia, chief people and experience officer, Prudential

claims.claim: Most startup managers burn out because they carry a full management load plus complex individual work done on nights and weekends
Writer and Databricks are moving to smaller teams rather than larger spans of control, because large spans only work in stable eras
Companies terminated people because they assumed AI would do more of the work than it currently does
claims.attribution: An HR manager in the healthcare industry, quoted in Charter AI Pulse interviews

claims.claim: Prudential has an entrenched workforce with many employees at 25 to 30 years of tenure or more, and launches a personalized, function-specific learning program called Raise Your AI Q in November
